newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi signals bourse opening up with new fund.
newsitem.headline: Saudi signals bourse opening up with new fund.

text.p: Saudi Arabia is slowly opening its doors to international investors with a new equity fund in which foreigners can own units, but analysts said on Tuesday that a more significant foreign role was still some way off.
"It is the first step to test the water and see foreign reaction, some time after that the process will be widened," a Saudi investor told Reuters by telephone from Riyadh.

"This is a very good step. It is the first opportunity to open up to international capital. Pension fund managers worldwide would like exposure to the region," National Commercial Bank chief economist Henry Azzam said from Jeddah.

Saudi American Bank (SAMBA), 30 percent owned by Citibank, said it had received central bank approval to set up the Saudi Arabian Investment Fund Ltd -- the first fund to allow foreign participation in the Gulf's biggest bourse, which is so far restricted to Saudis and other Gulf Arabs.
The closed-end fund, the size of which has not yet been announced, will be listed on the London Stock Exchange.
Only Saudi nationals can hold shares in all of the over 70 local firms, capitalised at some $45 billion, listed in Riyadh.
Nationals of the other five Gulf states can own Saudi equities, excluding banks -- which account for about a third of market capitalisation -- and certain other stocks.
Analysts said Riyadh was likely to follow the example of markets in Asia, which have gradually allowed foreigners in.
"It will open up eventually," said a banker.
"This is the beginning, not the end. My feeling is that as the kingdom gets more integrated to the global economy, the trend will continue," Azzam said.
The move will also usher in similar funds, for which some banks are awaiting central bank approval, analysts added.
"It has opened up the eyes of a lot of banks, sending them scurrying around trying to find out what they can do," said one.
"It is significant for Saudi as it is the beginning of foreign investment. Most banks are looking at setting up similar feeder funds," said a Riyadh-based investment manager.

"The market is opening up in much the same way as India. The authorities first allow a controllable foreign investment in the stock market through closed-ended funds. SAMBA has stolen the march on other banks and I know at least two others who are planning similar funds, pending approval," he added.
The benefits of foreign participation are clear. It could stem the flow of billions of dollars remitted every year by the six million expatriates in the kingdom and improve liquidity.
Analysts say it could also lure back some of the $100 billion in Saudi private wealth estimated to be offshore.

"This is going to enhance the market. It will help bring in more money from abroad, improve liquidity and reflect in higher prices," said a Saudi investor, of the market where analysts say only about 10 shares are regularly dealt in big volumes.

Official data show 137.8 million shares worth 25.4 billion riyals ($6.8 billion) were traded last year. This compares to 25.7 billion shares worth $19.3 billion in nearby Kuwait, where at $22 billion, market capitalisation is half that of Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia is behind some of its neighbours in opening up. Oman already allows 49 percent foreign ownership and in Bahrain, foreigners resident in the country for at least two years are allowed limited investment in most listed firms. A handful of others are completely open.

"As more banks get the opportunity to provide this service, liquidity will be added. It will help support prices of firms which are doing well and bring to the market a new group of professional investors requiring more and better information. It will encourage companies to provide this," Azzam said.

Access to information in the kingdom is generally difficult and company disclosure levels are not as strict as in the West. "One problem is that disclosure standards have to be far more regulated to be acceptable to foreigners," one banker said.
Shares are currently dealt by computer and telephone in trading rooms in banks across the kingdom.
($1=3.75 riyals)
